title: The Zaydis of Yemen
hookLine: a Shia school of Yemen, close to Sunni schools in much law
carry: zaydis seek an imam who comes forward openly

cards: What does the word Shia mean? Party, or followers. Tradition gives the full phrase as shi'at Ali, the party of Ali, the Prophet's cousin and son-in-law.
But the party has more than one house. Yesterday's three sittings belong to the Twelvers. Today's house grew up in the highlands of Yemen, with law a visitor from a Sunni mosque would recognize.
Its people are named for one man, a great-grandson of Ali, who stood up in Kufa when he believed the rulers of his day had gone wrong. His name was Zayd.

teach.h: ZAYD IBN ALI ROSE IN KUFA.
teach.b: Zayd ibn Ali was a grandson of Husayn, the grandson of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. Tradition says he was known for learning and prayer, and that he rose against the Umayyad rulers in Kufa and was killed there.
Those who held to his example became the Zaydis. Next, what makes a leader. For Twelvers, the imams are named one by one, each designated by the one before, and the twelfth is in hiding.
Zaydi teaching draws the line differently.

teach.h: AN IMAM WHO COMES FORWARD OPENLY.
teach.b: An imam must be a descendant of Ali and Fatima, learned enough to judge, upright, and willing to come forward openly and call people to what is right.
The Qur'an speaks of a community that will "enjoin right conduct and forbid indecency." Zaydi scholars hear a duty there: a qualified leader doesn't wait in silence. Then the law.
In much of the law of prayer, fasting and trade, Zaydi rulings sit near the Sunni schools, and Zaydi scholars have long read and argued with Hanafi and Shafi'i books.
Tradition says Zayd himself refused to condemn the first caliphs, Abu Bakr and Umar: Ali was the better choice, he held, and the others still led.
That stance has made the Zaydis a kind of bridge, close to both neighbors and identical to neither. Last, the place.

For a long stretch of history, Zaydi imams led communities in the mountains of northern Yemen, around towns like Sa'dah and Sana'a. The school is still there, in the mosques and schools of those highlands.

how: Zaydi Muslims, found mainly in the northern highlands of Yemen, follow a Shia school named for Zayd ibn Ali; they hold that an imam must be a learned descendant of Ali and Fatima who comes forward openly, and their law is close to the Sunni schools in much.

games.q: by Zaydi teaching, what kind of person can be the imam?
o: anyone the people elect, from any family.
a learned, upright descendant of Ali and Fatima who comes forward openly.
only a hidden imam who will return.
games.why: Zaydis require descent from Ali and Fatima, learning, uprightness, and a willingness to call people openly. no hidden imam, no silent waiting.

practice: Find Yemen in your mind, at the bottom corner of the Arabian peninsula, the Red Sea to the west and the Gulf of Aden to the south, then go up, off the coast, into the mountains: terraced fields, stone towers, towns built high.
That's where the Zaydi school grew. If you pray, you can remember the people of Yemen in your prayer; if not, just rest on that mountain picture and breathe.

wordCard.voice: The Zaydis. A Shia school named for Zayd ibn Ali, rooted in the highlands of Yemen, with law close to the Sunni schools in much. Today's word.
